ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase; LV, left ventricular; SBP, systolic blood pressure; TG, triglycerides.To expand on these observations, we used semi-quantitative BAT data from our AI tool to establish associations between continuous clinical parameters and BAT activity. We found an inverse association between total BAT metabolic activity and glucose levels (P < 0.001), HbA1c (P = 0.006), systolic blood pressure (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3b), mean arterial blood pressure (P < 0.001) and BNP (P = 0.01) and a trend with diastolic blood pressure (P = 0.12) (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We did not observe statistically significant associations between total BAT activity and lipids (Extended Data Fig. 5c).Given the absence of large-scale studies linking BAT status with cardiac imaging in humans, and the association of BAT with higher carotid elasticity in a small prospective study24, we extracted available echocardiogram data from patients in our PSM cohort and performed association analyses. In alignment with previous findings25, patients with BAT had significantly lower left ventricular mass index (P < 0.001), left ventricular posterior wall thickness in diastole (LVPWD) (P < 0.001), relative wall thickness (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3c), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) and mitral valve E/e’ ratio, with no changes in ejection fraction, left atrial volume index and mitral valve E/A ratio (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Similarly, increasing BAT metabolic activity was associated inversely with PASP (P < 0.001), LVPWD (P = 0.01), relative wall thickness (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3d), mitral valve E/e’ ratio (P = 0.002) and positively with mitral valve E/A ratio (P < 0.001) (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Other echocardiographic parameters did not exhibit associations with semi-quantitative BAT activity (Extended Data Fig. 5e). These data demonstrate that BAT presence and activity associate with decreased markers of left ventricular remodelling.With regard to other medical conditions, patients with BAT had lower transaminase levels (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3e), lower alkaline phosphatase and higher albumin, and a lower percentage of patients had increased FIB-4 scores—a surrogate for the risk of advanced liver fibrosis26 (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Parameters of systemic inflammation were also lower in patients with BAT, including total neutrophils (P < 0.001), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3e), platelets and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Extended Data Fig. 5g). There was also a trend towards lower C-reactive protein in patients with BAT, with no changes in total white blood cells or lymphocytes (Extended Data Fig. 5g). We did not observe changes in renal or thyroid function in patients in the BAT+ versus BAT− groups (Extended Data Fig. 5h). As patients with BAT showed a trend towards higher osteoporosis prevalence, available bone density scans were analysed. Patients with BAT had lower vertebral T-scores compared with patients in the BAT− group (P = 0.0026), with no changes in femoral neck T-scores (Fig. 3f).Pharmacological regulators of BATTo unravel pharmacologic determinants of BAT presence, we extracted home medication data 1 month before the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 6a). In total, 125 individual medications were assessed for associations with BAT status after exclusions (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Multi-variable logistic regression analyses identified that 39 of 125 medications exhibited a significant association with BAT status (Supplementary Table 6). Given that antibiotics are generally used in short courses, we excluded them from our list of chronic medications (Extended Data Fig. 6b). However, as modulation of the microbiome by antimicrobials could affect thermogenic fat27, we performed a focused analysis on antibiotics and found that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and several cephalosporins had positive associations with BAT status (Extended Data Fig. 6b).Among our 39 candidate medications, we identified agents with known inhibitory effects on human BAT, such as β-blockers9,28. Specifically, atenolol (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.27–0.64; P < 0.001) and propranolol (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20–0.74; P = 0.02) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6c) exhibited negative associations with BAT presence. Other known negative regulators of BAT, namely, selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)29 such as fluoxetine (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.21–0.51; P < 0.001), escitalopram (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48–0.75; P < 0.001) and sertraline (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.44–0.75; P < 0.001) (Fig. 4a), were also associated negatively with BAT. Given that people with BAT had a lower prevalence of psychiatric disease, we performed analyses on psychiatric medications controlling for relevant psychiatric diagnoses (Supplementary Table 7), and demonstrated that SSRIs retain their negative association with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d). Among medications shown previously to activate BAT, we found that dexamethasone30 was associated positively with BAT presence (OR 1.22; 95% CI 1.10–1.36; P = 0.001; Fig. 4a). Mirabegron—a β3-adrenergic agonist that promotes BAT activity in humans13,31,32—also showed a trend towards being associated with BAT positivity (Extended Data Fig. 6e). β2-adrenergic agonists (for example, inhaled salbutamol), which could promote BAT activity in humans33,34, did not show a significant association (Supplementary Table 6). Based on expression of the target receptor and/or pathway in adipocytes35, we focused on angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) as potential BAT-promoting drugs. The ARBs losartan (OR 1.36; 95% CI 1.13–1.63; P = 0.006) and valsartan (OR 1.52; 95% CI 1.14–2.02; P = 0.02) had significant positive associations with BAT+ status, whereas irbesartan exhibited a non-statistically significant trend in the same direction (Fig. 4b).Losartan enhances BAT activity through PPARγAs proof of concept, we tested whether losartan increased the activity of differentiated brown adipocytes in vitro. First, we assessed whether losartan regulated uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1)—the main mediator of BAT thermogenesis. Losartan at low doses (10 μM) had no effect, whereas higher doses (50 μM and 100 μM) significantly increased Ucp1 RNA levels in immortalized mature brown adipocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Treatment with losartan at 50 μM induced an increase in Ucp1 comparable with noradrenaline (NE)—a β-adrenergic agonist and known thermogenic activator (Fig. 4c); moreover, co-treatment with losartan and NE produced a synergistic effect on Ucp1 (Fig. 4c). Losartan also increased RNA levels of other thermogenic genes such as Pgc1a (also known as Ppargc1a), Elovl3 and Cidea (Extended Data Fig. 7b). A similar effect was seen in subcutaneous adipocytes enriched for beige adipocyte progenitors and, to a lesser extent, subcutaneous white adipocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Losartan increased UCP1 protein in primary mature brown adipocytes at baseline and upon NE stimulation (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 7d). Finally, we assessed oxygen consumption rate in primary mature brown adipocytes and demonstrated that 72 h pretreatment with losartan significantly increased NE-dependent uncoupled respiration—a proxy for thermogenesis (Fig. 4e).Similar to reports in human adipocytes36, angiotensin II decreased Ucp1 expression in mature brown adipocytes, whereas co-treatment with losartan rescued and further increased Ucp1 expression, suggesting a possible angiotensin receptor 1 (AT1R)-independent mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 7e). We treated mature brown adipocytes with EXP3174, the active losartan metabolite (10–40% higher affinity for ATR1 than the parent compound) and EXP3179—a losartan metabolite with no affinity for ATR1 (refs. 37,38). Unexpectedly, EXP3179, but not EXP3174, increased Ucp1 expression at baseline and in response to NE (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). To further confirm that losartan acts independently of AT1R signalling, we knocked down At1r (Extended Data Fig. 7h) and showed that losartan still increased Ucp1 expression. Knockdown of the receptor alone also seemed to affect Ucp1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 7i), consistent with both AT1R-dependent and independent mechanisms.Previous studies have suggested that some ARBs could act as direct PPARγ agonists39. We found that losartan and the inactive metabolite EXP3179, but not the active metabolite EXP3174, increased RNA levels of the classic PPARγ target aP2 with and without NE stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 7j–l). Losartan also decreased RNA levels of PPARγ with no changes to adiponectin (Extended Data Fig. 7m) Thus, using a luciferase reporter system in HEK293T cells, we tested whether losartan and its inactive metabolite EXP3179 activate PPARγ directly. Increasing concentrations of losartan or EXP3179, but not EXP3174, resulted in augmented reporter activity (Fig. 4f). To test directly whether PPARγ mediates the increased Ucp1 observed with losartan and EXP3179 in brown adipocytes, we co-treated cells with these compounds and a pharmacological inhibitor of PPARγ, GW9662, which binds the ligand-binding domain and prevents agonist-induced activation. Indeed, blocking PPARγ significantly attenuated the effects of losartan and its inactive metabolite on Ucp1 RNA induction at baseline and upon NE stimulation (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 7n,o). Altogether, these data demonstrate that losartan increases UCP1 expression in brown adipocytes independently of AT1R signalling and by stimulating PPARγ transcriptional activity.Finally, we investigated the effects of losartan on BAT physiology in vivo. Treating wild-type mice for 2 weeks with losartan at room temperature resulted in increased expression of Ucp1 and other thermogenic genes in BAT with no significant changes to adipogenesis genes (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). This was also observed at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). To functionally assess BAT thermogenic capacity, we acclimated losartan-treated mice and controls to thermoneutrality and then treated them acutely with the β3-agonist CL-316,243 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). BAT thermogenesis in response to β3 agonism (assessed by thermal camera) was higher in mice also receiving losartan compared with controls (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8f).To further assess the effects of losartan on whole-body energy expenditure, indirect calorimetry was performed in wild-type mice pre-treated with losartan in their drinking water for 10 days at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Losartan-treated mice exhibited increased energy expenditure, O2 consumption and CO2 production, with no changes to their respiratory exchange ratio (RER), physical activity, food intake, body weight, fat mass or lean mass (Extended Data Fig. 9a–l). To examine the effects of losartan on cold stress, we pre-treated a separate cohort of wild-type mice at room temperature as above and performed indirect calorimetry at 4 °C (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Upon cold-induced BAT activation, losartan-treated mice again exhibited increased energy expenditure, O2 consumption and CO2 production, with no changes in RER (Fig. 4j,k and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e). This was independent of body weight, as assayed by analysis of covariance (Fig. 4l). There were no differences in locomotor activity and a trend towards increased food intake in losartan-treated mice (Extended Data Fig. 10f–h), which probably explains why body weight did not change (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Moreover, exposing mice treated with losartan to cold resulted in significantly increased BAT Ucp1 (Fig. 4m), as well as smaller lipid droplets in brown adipocytes (Fig. 4n). We observed similar histologic findings in inguinal fat; however, there was no statistically significant increase in Ucp1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Taken together, these data indicate that losartan treatment results in enhanced BAT activation and increased whole-body energy expenditure.DiscussionDespite substantial advances, the therapeutic potential for targeting BAT to manage metabolic disease remains preliminary5,6. This retrospective study explored associations between BAT and human health in the largest cohort reported so far. We validated the strong link between BAT and cardiovascular diseases, while uncovering a previously undescribed association with psychiatric diseases. Our new machine learning approach allowed us to quantify depot-specific BAT metabolic activity rapidly and establish that the degree of BAT activity is linked to cardiometabolic health and healthier fat distribution. Finally, medication usage analysis uncovered a positive association between ARB use and BAT presence. Proof-of-concept in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that losartan activates brown adipocytes and promotes whole-body energy expenditure, demonstrating that our systems approach can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate BAT.Numerous studies in mice have shown that BAT activation protects against obesity and hyperglycaemia through increased energy expenditure, clearance of circulating substrates and secretion of beneficial hormones and metabolites40,41,42. In humans, cold exposure and β-adrenergic agonists increase BAT metabolic activity, which correlates with improved glucose homeostasis13,14. Our study confirms that, among all diagnoses, BAT is associated primarily with decreased prevalence of cardiovascular diseases, improved glycaemic, lipid and inflammatory profiles, and evidence of decreased pathological cardiac remodelling. Our large-scale, depot-specific analysis allowed us to identify axillary BAT as being linked most strongly with beneficial metabolic outcomes and healthier WAT distribution. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of thermogenic adipose tissues in humans and the importance of dissecting their cellular and molecular characteristics20,21,22.AI tools such as ours will allow other groups to analyse BAT semi-quantitatively in their cohorts and expand these findings to other populations worldwide. This approach continues to rely on BAT glucose uptake on 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans, which may or may not correlate with BAT temperature and thermogenic capacity43,44, and could be influenced significantly by insulin resistance45. To this point, we found that insulin-sensitizing medications such as metformin46 were associated negatively with BAT presence (adjusting for diabetes status), and medications like olanzapine47, which promote insulin resistance, were linked positively to BAT. This indicates that the clinical findings in our study cannot be explained simply by altered insulin sensitivity.Beyond metabolic diseases, BAT presence was associated with a lower prevalence of anxiety and depression. This could be explained by studies linking healthier metabolic profiles and decreased visceral adiposity to lower rates of psychiatric disease48,49,50. Small studies have linked cold exposure—a known activator of BAT—to improved mental health51,52. Furthermore, BAT prevalence decreased with SSRI use, confirming findings from a recent, prospective human study29. Future studies focused on how BAT affects mood and behaviour, and the role of anti-depressants in this crosstalk are warranted. BAT presence was associated with lower prevalence of liver disease and improved hepatic function, consistent with previous studies53,54. Conversely, patients in the BAT+ group showed a trend towards higher prevalence of osteoporosis and decreased lumbar bone mineral density, contrasting with previous reports linking cold-activated BAT with higher bone mineral density55. Although mouse studies suggest an endocrine connection between brown fat and bone56, we cannot rule out that the observed association is specific to our cancer-centre-based cohort. Future trials on human BAT therapeutics should include assessment of bone health.Our study uses a reverse translational approach, starting with a large human dataset that informs proof-of-concept experiments, to bridge the gap between predominantly mouse-based discoveries and human brown fat biology. Through this platform, we identified several ARBs that are associated positively with BAT and demonstrate that the medication used most widely in this family, losartan, directly activates brown adipocytes through PPARγ, independently of AT1R signalling. In vivo treatment with losartan at baseline and during a cold challenge resulted in increased whole-body energy expenditure. By contrast, a previous report described a role for losartan in beiging of white fat through AT1R-dependent apelin secretion57. Compared with losartan, its inactive metabolite EXP3179 exhibits higher PPARγ agonism in vitro, and it probably mediates most of the effects of losartan on BAT in vivo. In humans, chronic treatment with losartan resulted in increased serum levels of EXP3179 with a peak 2 h after treatment, and increased expression of PPARγ gene targets in circulating monocytes37. Treatment with ARBs has been associated with reductions in newly diagnosed diabetes58, which could be linked to its effects on brown fat.Our study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design highlights the need for large prospective studies; however, we controlled for several clinical confounders and validated the association of losartan with BAT experimentally. Second, 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans were obtained without previous cold exposure, potentially underestimating BAT prevalence. Third, our convenience cohort was derived from a cancer centre and, despite controlling extensively for cancer-related variables, we cannot exclude effects from tumour types or cancer therapies. For instance, BAT is linked to higher breast cancer prevalence, lower odds of gastrointestinal malignancies and higher usage of cancer treatments such as mitotic inhibitors. Studies in mice have suggested activation of BAT reduces cancer progression by decreasing available circulating glucose for tumour metabolism59. To our knowledge, there is no literature demonstrating direct effects of mitotic inhibitors or other cancer therapies on brown adipocytes, and future studies of these associations are warranted. Until a reliable biomarker or non-invasive test for BAT is established, a large, prospective study involving 18F-FDG-PET–CT in the non-oncologic setting is highly implausible. At present, a large PSM cohort is the most feasible approach to assess BAT and clinical phenotypes comprehensively in humans.In conclusion, we describe new associations between BAT and clinical outcomes through big data and AI-based analyses. Our systems-approach provides a resource for the field and can be extended to study other regulators of BAT such as genetics. Finally, our proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that losartan activates brown adipocytes through a PPARγ dependent mechanism, raising the possibility that this agent could be repurposed to activate BAT in humans.MethodsStudy design and participantsThis retrospective case–control study followed institutional guidelines and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), protocol number 17-581. The requirement for informed consent was waived because the study involved secondary analysis of previously acquired PET–CT imaging and clinical data, posed no more than minimal risk to participants and could not be conducted practically with individual informed consent. All patient data were deidentified before use.We previously established a cohort of patients with BAT by analysing 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from June 2009 through March 20184. Patients who were positive for BAT in at least one scan were termed BAT+, whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT−. To expand this cohort, we established a new Extension BAT Cohort by following a similar strategy. We reviewed all 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from patients aged 18 years and above from April 2018 through July 2024. People who were positive for BAT on at least one scan were termed BAT+, whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT− (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2). For each patient in both groups, an index scan was designated: in patients with BAT reported on at least one 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan, the first scan that reported BAT was defined as the index scan. In patients without BAT on any scan, the first 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan served as the index scan. We collected demographic, BMI, outside temperature data and pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases4 (1 year after the index scan) (Supplementary Table 8) from the institutional EHR. Average outdoor temperatures in New York City were obtained from the US National Weather Service. An initial logistic regression analysis was performed on patients in the BAT+ versus BAT− groups who belonged exclusively to the Extension BAT Cohort to establish associations between BAT presence and cardiometabolic diseases. As the association of BAT presence with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease was confirmed in the Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b), we proceeded to merge the Established BAT Cohort with the Extension BAT Cohort to create an Expanded BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a). If a patient was present in both cohorts, data from the Established BAT Cohort were used.Data collection and PSMTo create a balanced study cohort derived from the Expanded BAT Cohort, patients in the BAT+ and BAT− groups were matched using PSM. Propensity scores were estimated using a non-parsimonious multi-variable logistic regression model with BAT status (presence or absence) as the dependent variable and age, sex, BMI and temperature at time of scan as co-variates. Matching was performed using a greedy nearest neighbour matching algorithm without replacement, with a calliper width set to 0.2 and a matching ratio of 1:2. This resulted in a final study cohort of 26,302 (8,897 BAT+ and 17,405 BAT−). Balance diagnostics were performed to assess the success of the matching procedure using standardized mean differences for all variables included in the propensity score model before and after matching. Postmatching standardized mean differences within the range of −0.10 to 0.10 indicated adequate balance between the BAT+ and BAT− groups across all measured co-variates, supporting the validity of the PSM design for causal inference.We collected pertinent clinical data for each patient as described previously4. Pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases4 (Supplementary Table 8) and all other codes were extracted up to 1 year after the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort. A total of 104 codes were associated significantly with BAT status in this analysis. Subsequently, we analysed each of these 104 codes using a multi-variable regression analysis to assess their individual association with BAT, while controlling for age, sex, BMI, ambient temperature, self-reported race and ethnicity, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer site, cancer stage, cancer treatment and general groups of outpatient medications (Extended Data Fig. 1a).Machine learning approach to quantify BAT activityThe 3DF workflow19 used PET and CT images in DICOM format. Using information from the DICOM header regarding image orientation and patient spatial positioning, the PET image was resampled to match the dimensions of the CT image through linear interpolation. Both PET and CT images were then converted into the .nrrd file format and processed by nnU-net. The nnU-net model produced a mask prediction where each pixel value corresponds to an anatomical site: 1 for cervical, 2 for supraclavicular, 3 for mediastinal, 4 for paraspinal, 5 for axillary and 6 for abdominal regions. The mask predictions were interpreted by 3DF, and contours were generated. These contours were down-sampled to match the original PET image dimensions, and metrics from the original PET for each anatomical site were exported to an Excel master file. The 3DF process was executed in batch mode, with several instances running simultaneously to efficiently segment a large cohort. We used this method to quantify BAT metabolic activity in 8,709 patients in the BAT+ group from our cohort. The target slice was identified automatically using TotalSegmentator61 vertebral segmentation, with the analysis slice defined as the midpoint between the inferior extent of the L3 mask and the superior extent of the L4 mask. The outer body contour on the selected slice was derived by thresholding voxels above −500 Hounsfield units, followed by hole filling, removal of small components, retention of the largest connected component and morphological closing. Outer abdominal circumference was then calculated from the resulting body boundary using DICOM pixel spacing. Adipose tissue was quantified using a hybrid attenuation and AI-based method. Fat voxels were first identified within the body contour using an attenuation range of −195 to −45 Hounsfield units, and these voxels were then partitioned into SAT and VAT using TotalSegmentator tissue-type compartment masks. The outer abdominal circumference (in centimetres), SAT area (in square centimetres), VAT area (in square centimetres) and subcutaneous-to-visceral ratio were exported to an Excel master file. Post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Tukey’s HSD method. Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test.Associations between BAT and individual medications were assessed through multi-variable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI, temperature, ethnicity, race, smoking history, family history of cardiovascular disease, cancer sites, cancer stage, cancer treatment and cardiovascular diagnoses. For in vitro and in vivo proof-of-concept experiments, group comparisons were conducted using unpaired t-tests. To account for multiple comparisons, P values were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR method, and adjusted P values are reported as such where applicable. Metabolic cage data were analysed, and statistical significance was calculated either using two-way analysis of variance for hourly data or unpaired t-test for 24-h cumulative, light and dark cycle. All analyses were performed using SAS (v.9.4), R software (v.4.5.1) and GraphPad Prism (v.10.5.0). All reported P values are two-sided and statistical significance was defined as α < 0.05.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article. blocks.html_en: Main

Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension and cardiovascular disease2,7. Adipose tissue dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity and contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiometabolic diseases1. White adipose tissue (WAT) stores energy as triglyceride1 in subcutaneous and visceral depots, and visceral adiposity is a key feature of metabolically unhealthy obesity8. By contrast, brown adipose tissue (BAT) dissipates energy as heat (thermogenesis) and its activation in animal models protects against obesity and metabolic diseases3. However, the relevance of BAT to adult human physiology and whether it can be targeted therapeutically remain unclear5,6.

sentences.en: Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension and cardiovascular disease2,7.
Adipose tissue dysfunction is a hallmark of obesity and contributes to the pathophysiology of cardiometabolic diseases1.
White adipose tissue (WAT) stores energy as triglyceride1 in subcutaneous and visceral depots, and visceral adiposity is a key feature of metabolically unhealthy obesity8.
By contrast, brown adipose tissue (BAT) dissipates energy as heat (thermogenesis) and its activation in animal models protects against obesity and metabolic diseases3.
However, the relevance of BAT to adult human physiology and whether it can be targeted therapeutically remain unclear5,6.

blocks.html_en: Since the landmark reports that adult humans have inducible BAT9,10,11,12, several clinical studies have aimed to recruit BAT through cold exposure or β-adrenergic agonists13,14,15,16,17. Although these interventions activate BAT and improve glucose homeostasis, their side effects and the small number of participants studied have limited their clinical impact5. More recently, our group described the largest reported cohort of people with BAT and demonstrated that the presence of BAT in 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)–computed tomography (CT) (18F-FDG-PET–CT) scans obtained for clinical purposes and without previous stimulation was associated with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease4. A caveat from this work is that patients were characterized based on BAT presence or absence, rather than by quantitative BAT metabolic activity. Like WAT, human BAT is localized in distinct anatomic depots18, but whether these depots uniquely affect health remains unknown. Moreover, most human BAT studies have focused on cardiometabolic outcomes, but how this tissue influences other organ systems and disease types remains largely unexplored. These limitations have hindered the identification of pharmacologic agents that promote BAT activity, and there are no approved, widely used medications to leverage the cardiometabolic benefits linked to this tissue.

sentences.en: Since the landmark reports that adult humans have inducible BAT9,10,11,12, several clinical studies have aimed to recruit BAT through cold exposure or β-adrenergic agonists13,14,15,16,17.
Although these interventions activate BAT and improve glucose homeostasis, their side effects and the small number of participants studied have limited their clinical impact5.

More recently, our group described the largest reported cohort of people with BAT and demonstrated that the presence of BAT in 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)–computed tomography (CT) (18F-FDG-PET–CT) scans obtained for clinical purposes and without previous stimulation was associated with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease4.
A caveat from this work is that patients were characterized based on BAT presence or absence, rather than by quantitative BAT metabolic activity.
Like WAT, human BAT is localized in distinct anatomic depots18, but whether these depots uniquely affect health remains unknown.
Moreover, most human BAT studies have focused on cardiometabolic outcomes, but how this tissue influences other organ systems and disease types remains largely unexplored.

These limitations have hindered the identification of pharmacologic agents that promote BAT activity, and there are no approved, widely used medications to leverage the cardiometabolic benefits linked to this tissue.

blocks.html_en: In this study we expanded our cohort to more than 100,000 patients and performed an unbiased, comprehensive analysis across all diagnostic codes to identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT presence. Furthermore, we harnessed artificial intelligence (AI) to semi-automatically quantify total and depot-specific BAT metabolic activity from 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans. This allowed us to investigate associations between specific BAT depots, WAT distribution and cardiometabolic outcomes. Finally, we combined these approaches with medication use analyses to identify pharmacologic regulators of BAT and performed proof-of-concept experiments to validate losartan as an activator of brown adipocytes through a unique, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ)-dependent mechanism.

This allowed us to investigate associations between specific BAT depots, WAT distribution and cardiometabolic outcomes.

Finally, we combined these approaches with medication use analyses to identify pharmacologic regulators of BAT and performed proof-of-concept experiments to validate losartan as an activator of brown adipocytes through a unique, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPARγ)-dependent mechanism.

blocks.html_en: To discover associations between BAT and diseases beyond the cardiometabolic system, we expanded our previously described cohort (Established BAT Cohort)4 by reviewing additional FDG-PET–CT scans taken from 2018 to 2024 at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Of these, 4.4% reported BAT presence and 4,778 patients (7.9%) had at least one scan positive for BAT (hereafter termed BAT positive (BAT+); Extended Data Fig. 1a). The remaining patients were designated BAT negative (BAT−). These newly identified participants were grouped in an Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a) that validated findings from our Established BAT Cohort4 demonstrating lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases in people who are BAT+ (Extended Data Fig. 1b). To increase statistical power, we merged the Established and Extension BAT Cohorts to create an Expanded BAT Cohort, consisting of 101,243 patients, of whom 8,897 were BAT+ and 92,346 were BAT−. Each patient was assigned an index scan as a reference point for clinical data collection (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Similar to previous findings4, BAT was more prevalent in women in the Expanded BAT Cohort, and its prevalence decreased with age, higher ambient temperature at the time of the scan and increasing body mass index (BMI) (Extended Data Fig. 1c–f).

sentences.en: To discover associations between BAT and diseases beyond the cardiometabolic system, we expanded our previously described cohort (Established BAT Cohort)4 by reviewing additional FDG-PET–CT scans taken from 2018 to 2024 at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
Of these, 4.4% reported BAT presence and 4,778 patients (7.9%) had at least one scan positive for BAT (hereafter termed BAT positive (BAT+); Extended Data Fig. 1a).
The remaining patients were designated BAT negative (BAT−).

These newly identified participants were grouped in an Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a) that validated findings from our Established BAT Cohort4 demonstrating lower prevalence of cardiometabolic diseases in people who are BAT+ (Extended Data Fig. 1b).
To increase statistical power, we merged the Established and Extension BAT Cohorts to create an Expanded BAT Cohort, consisting of 101,243 patients, of whom 8,897 were BAT+ and 92,346 were BAT−.
Each patient was assigned an index scan as a reference point for clinical data collection (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

Similar to previous findings4, BAT was more prevalent in women in the Expanded BAT Cohort, and its prevalence decreased with age, higher ambient temperature at the time of the scan and increasing body mass index (BMI) (Extended Data Fig. 1c–f).

blocks.html_en: Given the influence of these variables on BAT prevalence, we used propensity score matching (PSM) to create a cohort of patients in the BAT+ (n = 8,897) and BAT− (n = 17,405) groups balanced across age, sex, BMI and ambient temperature (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h). As patients in our cohort come from a cancer centre, we extracted extensive cancer-associated data (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2) for each patient in our PSM cohort, including site, stage and treatment. We confirmed that certain cancer sites were more frequent (for example, breast and oral cavity), less frequent (for example, digestive) or had no association (for example, skin, urinary) with BAT presence (Table 1). As in our previous report, some cancer treatments were used more frequently in the BAT+ group4 (Table 1). Consequently, all cancer-associated variables were controlled for unless otherwise stated for the remainder of this study. We then performed multi-variable logistic regression in this new, expanded PSM cohort and confirmed the association between BAT presence and decreased prevalence of select cardiometabolic diseases4 (Extended Data Fig. 1i). Given the sexual dimorphism in BAT presence and cardiometabolic traits, we performed separate analyses in women and men and found that BAT was associated with decreased odds of cardiometabolic diseases in both sexes in our PSM and Extension BAT Cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b).

blocks.html_en: Next, we used an unbiased approach to establish associations between BAT and diseases across all organ systems in our PSM cohort (Fig. 1a). After extraction of International Classification of Diseases (ICD) code data and initial screening analysis (Fig. 1a), 104 of 511 codes exhibited significant, non-adjusted associations with BAT (Supplementary Table 3). Over-representation analysis revealed that cardiovascular and psychiatric diagnoses were enriched significantly in their association with BAT (Fig. 1b). We then ran a multi-variable logistic regression for each of the 104 codes to establish associations with BAT, adjusting for multiple co-variates. This resulted in 98 codes that were significant after adjustment, with 92 showing lower incidence in patients in the BAT+ group (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 4).

blocks.html_en: Among the top 20 codes with lower prevalence in the BAT+ group, the two most significant were T2D (odds ratio (OR) 0.42; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.35–0.50; P < 0.001) and chronic ischaemic heart disease (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.44–0.62; P < 0.001); other cardiometabolic codes such as disorders of lipoprotein metabolism (OR 0.76; 95% CI 0.70–0.83; P < 0.001) and primary hypertension (OR 0.79; 95% CI 0.73–0.85; P < 0.001) were also present. We also identified associations with other disease systems, including decreased odds of respiratory failure (OR 0.46; 95% CI 0.37–0.57; P < 0.001), ascites (OR 0.51; 95% CI 0.43–0.62; P < 0.001), anxiety disorders (OR 0.78; 95% CI 0.73–0.84; P < 0.001), depressive episode (OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.61–0.76; P < 0.001) and sleep disorders (OR 0.77; 95% CI 0.71–0.85; P < 0.001) in patients who were BAT+ (Fig. 1c). Among codes with higher prevalence in the BAT+ group, five of six were skin diagnoses (Extended Data Fig. 2c). BAT+ status also trended toward being associated with a higher prevalence of osteoporosis, although this did not reach statistical significance in the adjusted analysis (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

blocks.html_en: We used a newly developed machine learning-based approach (TriDFusion (3DF))19 to semi-automatically measure total and depot-specific BAT metabolic activity (defined as product of the mean standard 18F-FDG uptake value (standardized uptake value (SUV)) and BAT volume in millilitres) from most patients with BAT+ status (n = 8,709; 97.9% of the BAT+ group (Methods)) in our Expanded BAT Cohort (Fig. 2a,b). Among the six previously described BAT depots, the supraclavicular had the highest prevalence and activity (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Total BAT metabolic activity was correlated inversely with age and was higher in women (Extended Data Fig. 3c–f). As cardiometabolic diagnoses exhibited the strongest link with BAT (Fig. 1b), we stratified our 8,709 patients with BAT activity measurements into tertiles and examined whether increasing total and depot-specific BAT activity was associated with decreased odds of cardiometabolic diseases using patients in the BAT− group as a reference. Indeed, higher total BAT metabolic activity was associated with a stepwise reduction in the prevalence of T2D (P < 0.001), atrial fibrillation and/or atrial flutter (P < 0.001), coronary artery disease (CAD; P < 0.001) and congestive heart failure (P < 0.001), even after controlling for age, BMI, sex and outside temperature (Fig. 2c).

Among the six previously described BAT depots, the supraclavicular had the highest prevalence and activity (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b).
Total BAT metabolic activity was correlated inversely with age and was higher in women (Extended Data Fig. 3c–f).

blocks.html_en: BAT in humans is localized in several depots, which could have distinct functions depending on their location or could contain different cell types20,21,22. Until now, it was not feasible to perform large-scale analyses with depot-level resolution, so we used our AI tool to compare the association between cardiometabolic diagnoses and BAT metabolic activity in each of the six different BAT depots compared with patients in the BAT− group (Fig. 2c). Within the most prevalent depot, the supraclavicular, increasing BAT activity was associated with clear, dose-dependent reduced odds of T2D (P < 0.001) and CAD (P < 0.001) in all tertiles. In both the cervical and supraclavicular depots, higher BAT activity was associated with lower odds of hypertension, but this effect was lost for patients with highest BAT activity (tertile 3) (Fig. 2c). Of note, increasing axillary BAT activity was associated with significant reductions in the prevalence of all cardiometabolic diseases queried (including cerebrovascular disease), with a clear stepwise decrease in the risk of hypertension, in contrast to most other depots (Fig. 2c).

sentences.en: BAT in humans is localized in several depots, which could have distinct functions depending on their location or could contain different cell types20,21,22.

Until now, it was not feasible to perform large-scale analyses with depot-level resolution, so we used our AI tool to compare the association between cardiometabolic diagnoses and BAT metabolic activity in each of the six different BAT depots compared with patients in the BAT− group (Fig. 2c).
Within the most prevalent depot, the supraclavicular, increasing BAT activity was associated with clear, dose-dependent reduced odds of T2D (P < 0.001) and CAD (P < 0.001) in all tertiles.

In both the cervical and supraclavicular depots, higher BAT activity was associated with lower odds of hypertension, but this effect was lost for patients with highest BAT activity (tertile 3) (Fig. 2c).

Of note, increasing axillary BAT activity was associated with significant reductions in the prevalence of all cardiometabolic diseases queried (including cerebrovascular disease), with a clear stepwise decrease in the risk of hypertension, in contrast to most other depots (Fig. 2c).

blocks.html_en: We carried out similarly controlled analyses within patients with BAT+ status, using patients in tertile 1 as a reference. Given the low prevalence of cardiometabolic disease in people with BAT, the associations were not as statistically powerful, but we identified similar trends (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Increasing total BAT metabolic activity was associated with lower odds of T2D (P = 0.009) and CAD (P = 0.03) in this analysis. Within the cervical depot, higher BAT activity was associated with a slight reduction in the incidence of CAD (P = 0.04), but increased odds of hypertension (P < 0.001). Increasing mediastinal BAT activity was associated exclusively with reduced CAD prevalence (P = 0.004)—an interesting finding given its anatomical location. Of note, higher axillary BAT activity also showed the greatest effects in this analysis, associating with reductions in T2D (P = 0.03), congestive heart failure (P = 0.02) and hypertension (P = 0.005) (Extended Data Fig. 3g).

Of note, higher axillary BAT activity also showed the greatest effects in this analysis, associating with reductions in T2D (P = 0.03), congestive heart failure (P = 0.02) and hypertension (P = 0.005) (Extended Data Fig. 3g).

blocks.html_en: Given the well described association between WAT distribution and cardiometabolic disease8, we used the CT portion of each 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan to semi-automatically measure the subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) area. We were able to obtain these measurements and the SAT to VAT ratio in 8,040 patients in the BAT+ group (92.3% of patients with BAT from our PSM cohort; Extended Data Fig. 4a). We then performed linear regression analyses between BAT activity and WAT distribution parameters. From here on, most variables were log transformed due to non-normal data distribution and, consequently, coefficients (β) derived from the linear regression appear numerically small, as they reflect proportional relationships rather than raw changes. Total BAT metabolic activity showed a positive association with SAT area (P < 0.001), negative association with VAT area (P < 0.001) and positive association with SAT to VAT ratio (Fig. 2d,e). Given our previous findings, we assessed the association between depot-specific BAT activity and WAT distribution. Supraclavicular (Extended Data Fig. 4b,c), mediastinal (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g) and abdominal (Extended Data Fig. 4j,k) BAT metabolic activity behaved similarly to total BAT, exhibiting positive associations with SAT area and SAT to VAT ratio, and negative associations with VAT area. Paraspinal (Extended Data Fig. 4h,i) and cervical (Extended Data Fig. 4d,e) BAT (the latter exhibiting an association with increased odds of hypertension) were associated positively with SAT and VAT. Finally, axillary BAT (Fig. 2f,g), which was associated most strongly with decreased odds of cardiometabolic diseases, exhibited the most significant negative association with VAT area and, consequently, the strongest positive association with SAT to VAT ratio. Collectively, these data highlight the unique phenotypes linked to different BAT depots.

blocks.html_en: To further investigate clinical correlates of BAT we extracted an expanded battery of available laboratory tests and imaging studies from patients in our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 5a) and performed analyses to identify differences between patients in the BAT+ and BAT− groups (Supplementary Table 5). Patients with BAT had lower glucose (P < 0.001), haemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) (P < 0.001), triglycerides (P < 0.001) and triglyceride-glucose index, as well as higher high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol (HDL-C) levels (P < 0.001), even after adjusting for confounders (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 5b). Paradoxically, patients with BAT also had higher total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). However, remnant cholesterol (total cholesterol − LDL − HDL)—an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease23—was significantly lower in patients with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Finally, patients with BAT exhibited lower circulating brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) (Extended Data Fig. 5b).

blocks.html_en: To expand on these observations, we used semi-quantitative BAT data from our AI tool to establish associations between continuous clinical parameters and BAT activity. We found an inverse association between total BAT metabolic activity and glucose levels (P < 0.001), HbA1c (P = 0.006), systolic blood pressure (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3b), mean arterial blood pressure (P < 0.001) and BNP (P = 0.01) and a trend with diastolic blood pressure (P = 0.12) (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We did not observe statistically significant associations between total BAT activity and lipids (Extended Data Fig. 5c).

sentences.en: To expand on these observations, we used semi-quantitative BAT data from our AI tool to establish associations between continuous clinical parameters and BAT activity.

We found an inverse association between total BAT metabolic activity and glucose levels (P < 0.001), HbA1c (P = 0.006), systolic blood pressure (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3b), mean arterial blood pressure (P < 0.001) and BNP (P = 0.01) and a trend with diastolic blood pressure (P = 0.12) (Extended Data Fig. 5c).
We did not observe statistically significant associations between total BAT activity and lipids (Extended Data Fig. 5c).

blocks.html_en: Given the absence of large-scale studies linking BAT status with cardiac imaging in humans, and the association of BAT with higher carotid elasticity in a small prospective study24, we extracted available echocardiogram data from patients in our PSM cohort and performed association analyses. In alignment with previous findings25, patients with BAT had significantly lower left ventricular mass index (P < 0.001), left ventricular posterior wall thickness in diastole (LVPWD) (P < 0.001), relative wall thickness (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3c), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) and mitral valve E/e’ ratio, with no changes in ejection fraction, left atrial volume index and mitral valve E/A ratio (Extended Data Fig. 5d). Similarly, increasing BAT metabolic activity was associated inversely with PASP (P < 0.001), LVPWD (P = 0.01), relative wall thickness (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3d), mitral valve E/e’ ratio (P = 0.002) and positively with mitral valve E/A ratio (P < 0.001) (Extended Data Fig. 5e). Other echocardiographic parameters did not exhibit associations with semi-quantitative BAT activity (Extended Data Fig. 5e). These data demonstrate that BAT presence and activity associate with decreased markers of left ventricular remodelling.

Similarly, increasing BAT metabolic activity was associated inversely with PASP (P < 0.001), LVPWD (P = 0.01), relative wall thickness (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3d), mitral valve E/e’ ratio (P = 0.002) and positively with mitral valve E/A ratio (P < 0.001) (Extended Data Fig. 5e).
Other echocardiographic parameters did not exhibit associations with semi-quantitative BAT activity (Extended Data Fig. 5e).
These data demonstrate that BAT presence and activity associate with decreased markers of left ventricular remodelling.

blocks.html_en: With regard to other medical conditions, patients with BAT had lower transaminase levels (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3e), lower alkaline phosphatase and higher albumin, and a lower percentage of patients had increased FIB-4 scores—a surrogate for the risk of advanced liver fibrosis26 (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Parameters of systemic inflammation were also lower in patients with BAT, including total neutrophils (P < 0.001), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (P < 0.001) (Fig. 3e), platelets and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Extended Data Fig. 5g). There was also a trend towards lower C-reactive protein in patients with BAT, with no changes in total white blood cells or lymphocytes (Extended Data Fig. 5g). We did not observe changes in renal or thyroid function in patients in the BAT+ versus BAT− groups (Extended Data Fig. 5h). As patients with BAT showed a trend towards higher osteoporosis prevalence, available bone density scans were analysed. Patients with BAT had lower vertebral T-scores compared with patients in the BAT− group (P = 0.0026), with no changes in femoral neck T-scores (Fig. 3f).

blocks.html_en: Pharmacological regulators of BAT

sentences.en: Pharmacological regulators of BAT

blocks.html_en: To unravel pharmacologic determinants of BAT presence, we extracted home medication data 1 month before the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 6a). In total, 125 individual medications were assessed for associations with BAT status after exclusions (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Multi-variable logistic regression analyses identified that 39 of 125 medications exhibited a significant association with BAT status (Supplementary Table 6). Given that antibiotics are generally used in short courses, we excluded them from our list of chronic medications (Extended Data Fig. 6b). However, as modulation of the microbiome by antimicrobials could affect thermogenic fat27, we performed a focused analysis on antibiotics and found that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and several cephalosporins had positive associations with BAT status (Extended Data Fig. 6b).

sentences.en: To unravel pharmacologic determinants of BAT presence, we extracted home medication data 1 month before the index scan in patients from our PSM cohort (Extended Data Fig. 6a).
In total, 125 individual medications were assessed for associations with BAT status after exclusions (Extended Data Fig. 6a).
Multi-variable logistic regression analyses identified that 39 of 125 medications exhibited a significant association with BAT status (Supplementary Table 6).
Given that antibiotics are generally used in short courses, we excluded them from our list of chronic medications (Extended Data Fig. 6b).

However, as modulation of the microbiome by antimicrobials could affect thermogenic fat27, we performed a focused analysis on antibiotics and found that trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and several cephalosporins had positive associations with BAT status (Extended Data Fig. 6b).

blocks.html_en: Among our 39 candidate medications, we identified agents with known inhibitory effects on human BAT, such as β-blockers9,28. Specifically, atenolol (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.27–0.64; P < 0.001) and propranolol (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.20–0.74; P = 0.02) (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 6c) exhibited negative associations with BAT presence. Other known negative regulators of BAT, namely, selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)29 such as fluoxetine (OR 0.33; 95% CI 0.21–0.51; P < 0.001), escitalopram (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48–0.75; P < 0.001) and sertraline (OR 0.57; 95% CI 0.44–0.75; P < 0.001) (Fig. 4a), were also associated negatively with BAT. Given that people with BAT had a lower prevalence of psychiatric disease, we performed analyses on psychiatric medications controlling for relevant psychiatric diagnoses (Supplementary Table 7), and demonstrated that SSRIs retain their negative association with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d). Among medications shown previously to activate BAT, we found that dexamethasone30 was associated positively with BAT presence (OR 1.22; 95% CI 1.10–1.36; P = 0.001; Fig. 4a). Mirabegron—a β3-adrenergic agonist that promotes BAT activity in humans13,31,32—also showed a trend towards being associated with BAT positivity (Extended Data Fig. 6e). β2-adrenergic agonists (for example, inhaled salbutamol), which could promote BAT activity in humans33,34, did not show a significant association (Supplementary Table 6). These findings demonstrate that our platform can identify most known modulators of human BAT and could uncover new pharmacological regulators of this tissue.

Given that people with BAT had a lower prevalence of psychiatric disease, we performed analyses on psychiatric medications controlling for relevant psychiatric diagnoses (Supplementary Table 7), and demonstrated that SSRIs retain their negative association with BAT (Extended Data Fig. 6d).

Mirabegron—a β3-adrenergic agonist that promotes BAT activity in humans13,31,32—also showed a trend towards being associated with BAT positivity (Extended Data Fig. 6e). β2-adrenergic agonists (for example, inhaled salbutamol), which could promote BAT activity in humans33,34, did not show a significant association (Supplementary Table 6).

blocks.html_en: Among medications associated positively with BAT, we found hormonal modifiers (letrozole, leuprolide), antihypertensives (hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, losartan) and oral cancer drugs (osimertinib, lenalidomide). Based on expression of the target receptor and/or pathway in adipocytes35, we focused on angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) as potential BAT-promoting drugs. The ARBs losartan (OR 1.36; 95% CI 1.13–1.63; P = 0.006) and valsartan (OR 1.52; 95% CI 1.14–2.02; P = 0.02) had significant positive associations with BAT+ status, whereas irbesartan exhibited a non-statistically significant trend in the same direction (Fig. 4b).

blocks.html_en: Losartan enhances BAT activity through PPARγ

sentences.en: Losartan enhances BAT activity through PPARγ

blocks.html_en: As proof of concept, we tested whether losartan increased the activity of differentiated brown adipocytes in vitro. First, we assessed whether losartan regulated uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1)—the main mediator of BAT thermogenesis. Losartan at low doses (10 μM) had no effect, whereas higher doses (50 μM and 100 μM) significantly increased Ucp1 RNA levels in immortalized mature brown adipocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Treatment with losartan at 50 μM induced an increase in Ucp1 comparable with noradrenaline (NE)—a β-adrenergic agonist and known thermogenic activator (Fig. 4c); moreover, co-treatment with losartan and NE produced a synergistic effect on Ucp1 (Fig. 4c). Losartan also increased RNA levels of other thermogenic genes such as Pgc1a (also known as Ppargc1a), Elovl3 and Cidea (Extended Data Fig. 7b). A similar effect was seen in subcutaneous adipocytes enriched for beige adipocyte progenitors and, to a lesser extent, subcutaneous white adipocytes (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Losartan increased UCP1 protein in primary mature brown adipocytes at baseline and upon NE stimulation (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 7d). Finally, we assessed oxygen consumption rate in primary mature brown adipocytes and demonstrated that 72 h pretreatment with losartan significantly increased NE-dependent uncoupled respiration—a proxy for thermogenesis (Fig. 4e).

Finally, we assessed oxygen consumption rate in primary mature brown adipocytes and demonstrated that 72 h pretreatment with losartan significantly increased NE-dependent uncoupled respiration—a proxy for thermogenesis (Fig. 4e).

blocks.html_en: Similar to reports in human adipocytes36, angiotensin II decreased Ucp1 expression in mature brown adipocytes, whereas co-treatment with losartan rescued and further increased Ucp1 expression, suggesting a possible angiotensin receptor 1 (AT1R)-independent mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 7e). We treated mature brown adipocytes with EXP3174, the active losartan metabolite (10–40% higher affinity for ATR1 than the parent compound) and EXP3179—a losartan metabolite with no affinity for ATR1 (refs. 37,38). Unexpectedly, EXP3179, but not EXP3174, increased Ucp1 expression at baseline and in response to NE (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). To further confirm that losartan acts independently of AT1R signalling, we knocked down At1r (Extended Data Fig. 7h) and showed that losartan still increased Ucp1 expression. Knockdown of the receptor alone also seemed to affect Ucp1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 7i), consistent with both AT1R-dependent and independent mechanisms.

blocks.html_en: Previous studies have suggested that some ARBs could act as direct PPARγ agonists39. We found that losartan and the inactive metabolite EXP3179, but not the active metabolite EXP3174, increased RNA levels of the classic PPARγ target aP2 with and without NE stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 7j–l). Losartan also decreased RNA levels of PPARγ with no changes to adiponectin (Extended Data Fig. 7m) Thus, using a luciferase reporter system in HEK293T cells, we tested whether losartan and its inactive metabolite EXP3179 activate PPARγ directly. Increasing concentrations of losartan or EXP3179, but not EXP3174, resulted in augmented reporter activity (Fig. 4f). To test directly whether PPARγ mediates the increased Ucp1 observed with losartan and EXP3179 in brown adipocytes, we co-treated cells with these compounds and a pharmacological inhibitor of PPARγ, GW9662, which binds the ligand-binding domain and prevents agonist-induced activation. Indeed, blocking PPARγ significantly attenuated the effects of losartan and its inactive metabolite on Ucp1 RNA induction at baseline and upon NE stimulation (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 7n,o). Altogether, these data demonstrate that losartan increases UCP1 expression in brown adipocytes independently of AT1R signalling and by stimulating PPARγ transcriptional activity.

blocks.html_en: Finally, we investigated the effects of losartan on BAT physiology in vivo. Treating wild-type mice for 2 weeks with losartan at room temperature resulted in increased expression of Ucp1 and other thermogenic genes in BAT with no significant changes to adipogenesis genes (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). This was also observed at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). To functionally assess BAT thermogenic capacity, we acclimated losartan-treated mice and controls to thermoneutrality and then treated them acutely with the β3-agonist CL-316,243 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). BAT thermogenesis in response to β3 agonism (assessed by thermal camera) was higher in mice also receiving losartan compared with controls (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8f).

BAT thermogenesis in response to β3 agonism (assessed by thermal camera) was higher in mice also receiving losartan compared with controls (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8f).

blocks.html_en: To further assess the effects of losartan on whole-body energy expenditure, indirect calorimetry was performed in wild-type mice pre-treated with losartan in their drinking water for 10 days at room temperature (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Losartan-treated mice exhibited increased energy expenditure, O2 consumption and CO2 production, with no changes to their respiratory exchange ratio (RER), physical activity, food intake, body weight, fat mass or lean mass (Extended Data Fig. 9a–l). To examine the effects of losartan on cold stress, we pre-treated a separate cohort of wild-type mice at room temperature as above and performed indirect calorimetry at 4 °C (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Upon cold-induced BAT activation, losartan-treated mice again exhibited increased energy expenditure, O2 consumption and CO2 production, with no changes in RER (Fig. 4j,k and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e). This was independent of body weight, as assayed by analysis of covariance (Fig. 4l). There were no differences in locomotor activity and a trend towards increased food intake in losartan-treated mice (Extended Data Fig. 10f–h), which probably explains why body weight did not change (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Moreover, exposing mice treated with losartan to cold resulted in significantly increased BAT Ucp1 (Fig. 4m), as well as smaller lipid droplets in brown adipocytes (Fig. 4n). We observed similar histologic findings in inguinal fat; however, there was no statistically significant increase in Ucp1 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Taken together, these data indicate that losartan treatment results in enhanced BAT activation and increased whole-body energy expenditure.

blocks.html_en: Discussion

sentences.en: Discussion

blocks.html_en: Despite substantial advances, the therapeutic potential for targeting BAT to manage metabolic disease remains preliminary5,6. This retrospective study explored associations between BAT and human health in the largest cohort reported so far. We validated the strong link between BAT and cardiovascular diseases, while uncovering a previously undescribed association with psychiatric diseases. Our new machine learning approach allowed us to quantify depot-specific BAT metabolic activity rapidly and establish that the degree of BAT activity is linked to cardiometabolic health and healthier fat distribution. Finally, medication usage analysis uncovered a positive association between ARB use and BAT presence. Proof-of-concept in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that losartan activates brown adipocytes and promotes whole-body energy expenditure, demonstrating that our systems approach can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate BAT.

Finally, medication usage analysis uncovered a positive association between ARB use and BAT presence.

Proof-of-concept in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that losartan activates brown adipocytes and promotes whole-body energy expenditure, demonstrating that our systems approach can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate BAT.

blocks.html_en: Numerous studies in mice have shown that BAT activation protects against obesity and hyperglycaemia through increased energy expenditure, clearance of circulating substrates and secretion of beneficial hormones and metabolites40,41,42. In humans, cold exposure and β-adrenergic agonists increase BAT metabolic activity, which correlates with improved glucose homeostasis13,14. Our study confirms that, among all diagnoses, BAT is associated primarily with decreased prevalence of cardiovascular diseases, improved glycaemic, lipid and inflammatory profiles, and evidence of decreased pathological cardiac remodelling. Our large-scale, depot-specific analysis allowed us to identify axillary BAT as being linked most strongly with beneficial metabolic outcomes and healthier WAT distribution. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of thermogenic adipose tissues in humans and the importance of dissecting their cellular and molecular characteristics20,21,22.

These findings highlight the heterogeneity of thermogenic adipose tissues in humans and the importance of dissecting their cellular and molecular characteristics20,21,22.

blocks.html_en: AI tools such as ours will allow other groups to analyse BAT semi-quantitatively in their cohorts and expand these findings to other populations worldwide. This approach continues to rely on BAT glucose uptake on 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans, which may or may not correlate with BAT temperature and thermogenic capacity43,44, and could be influenced significantly by insulin resistance45. To this point, we found that insulin-sensitizing medications such as metformin46 were associated negatively with BAT presence (adjusting for diabetes status), and medications like olanzapine47, which promote insulin resistance, were linked positively to BAT. This indicates that the clinical findings in our study cannot be explained simply by altered insulin sensitivity.

blocks.html_en: Beyond metabolic diseases, BAT presence was associated with a lower prevalence of anxiety and depression. This could be explained by studies linking healthier metabolic profiles and decreased visceral adiposity to lower rates of psychiatric disease48,49,50. Small studies have linked cold exposure—a known activator of BAT—to improved mental health51,52. Furthermore, BAT prevalence decreased with SSRI use, confirming findings from a recent, prospective human study29. Future studies focused on how BAT affects mood and behaviour, and the role of anti-depressants in this crosstalk are warranted. BAT presence was associated with lower prevalence of liver disease and improved hepatic function, consistent with previous studies53,54. Conversely, patients in the BAT+ group showed a trend towards higher prevalence of osteoporosis and decreased lumbar bone mineral density, contrasting with previous reports linking cold-activated BAT with higher bone mineral density55. Although mouse studies suggest an endocrine connection between brown fat and bone56, we cannot rule out that the observed association is specific to our cancer-centre-based cohort. Future trials on human BAT therapeutics should include assessment of bone health.

blocks.html_en: Our study uses a reverse translational approach, starting with a large human dataset that informs proof-of-concept experiments, to bridge the gap between predominantly mouse-based discoveries and human brown fat biology. Through this platform, we identified several ARBs that are associated positively with BAT and demonstrate that the medication used most widely in this family, losartan, directly activates brown adipocytes through PPARγ, independently of AT1R signalling. In vivo treatment with losartan at baseline and during a cold challenge resulted in increased whole-body energy expenditure. By contrast, a previous report described a role for losartan in beiging of white fat through AT1R-dependent apelin secretion57. Compared with losartan, its inactive metabolite EXP3179 exhibits higher PPARγ agonism in vitro, and it probably mediates most of the effects of losartan on BAT in vivo. In humans, chronic treatment with losartan resulted in increased serum levels of EXP3179 with a peak 2 h after treatment, and increased expression of PPARγ gene targets in circulating monocytes37. Treatment with ARBs has been associated with reductions in newly diagnosed diabetes58, which could be linked to its effects on brown fat.

blocks.html_en: Our study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design highlights the need for large prospective studies; however, we controlled for several clinical confounders and validated the association of losartan with BAT experimentally. Second, 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans were obtained without previous cold exposure, potentially underestimating BAT prevalence. Third, our convenience cohort was derived from a cancer centre and, despite controlling extensively for cancer-related variables, we cannot exclude effects from tumour types or cancer therapies. For instance, BAT is linked to higher breast cancer prevalence, lower odds of gastrointestinal malignancies and higher usage of cancer treatments such as mitotic inhibitors. Studies in mice have suggested activation of BAT reduces cancer progression by decreasing available circulating glucose for tumour metabolism59. To our knowledge, there is no literature demonstrating direct effects of mitotic inhibitors or other cancer therapies on brown adipocytes, and future studies of these associations are warranted. Until a reliable biomarker or non-invasive test for BAT is established, a large, prospective study involving 18F-FDG-PET–CT in the non-oncologic setting is highly implausible. At present, a large PSM cohort is the most feasible approach to assess BAT and clinical phenotypes comprehensively in humans.

blocks.html_en: In conclusion, we describe new associations between BAT and clinical outcomes through big data and AI-based analyses. Our systems-approach provides a resource for the field and can be extended to study other regulators of BAT such as genetics. Finally, our proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that losartan activates brown adipocytes through a PPARγ dependent mechanism, raising the possibility that this agent could be repurposed to activate BAT in humans.

blocks.html_en: This retrospective case–control study followed institutional guidelines and was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK), protocol number 17-581. The requirement for informed consent was waived because the study involved secondary analysis of previously acquired PET–CT imaging and clinical data, posed no more than minimal risk to participants and could not be conducted practically with individual informed consent. All patient data were deidentified before use.

The requirement for informed consent was waived because the study involved secondary analysis of previously acquired PET–CT imaging and clinical data, posed no more than minimal risk to participants and could not be conducted practically with individual informed consent.

blocks.html_en: We previously established a cohort of patients with BAT by analysing 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from June 2009 through March 20184. Patients who were positive for BAT in at least one scan were termed BAT+, whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT−. To expand this cohort, we established a new Extension BAT Cohort by following a similar strategy. We reviewed all 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from patients aged 18 years and above from April 2018 through July 2024. People who were positive for BAT on at least one scan were termed BAT+, whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT− (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2). For each patient in both groups, an index scan was designated: in patients with BAT reported on at least one 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan, the first scan that reported BAT was defined as the index scan. In patients without BAT on any scan, the first 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan served as the index scan. We collected demographic, BMI, outside temperature data and pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases4 (1 year after the index scan) (Supplementary Table 8) from the institutional EHR. Average outdoor temperatures in New York City were obtained from the US National Weather Service. An initial logistic regression analysis was performed on patients in the BAT+ versus BAT− groups who belonged exclusively to the Extension BAT Cohort to establish associations between BAT presence and cardiometabolic diseases. As the association of BAT presence with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease was confirmed in the Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b), we proceeded to merge the Established BAT Cohort with the Extension BAT Cohort to create an Expanded BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a). If a patient was present in both cohorts, data from the Established BAT Cohort were used.

We reviewed all 18F-FDG-PET–CT scans performed at MSK from patients aged 18 years and above from April 2018 through July 2024.
People who were positive for BAT on at least one scan were termed BAT+, whereas the remaining patients were grouped as BAT− (Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 2).
For each patient in both groups, an index scan was designated: in patients with BAT reported on at least one 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan, the first scan that reported BAT was defined as the index scan.
In patients without BAT on any scan, the first 18F-FDG-PET–CT scan served as the index scan.

We collected demographic, BMI, outside temperature data and pertinent ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes corresponding to cardiometabolic diseases4 (1 year after the index scan) (Supplementary Table 8) from the institutional EHR.
Average outdoor temperatures in New York City were obtained from the US National Weather Service.

An initial logistic regression analysis was performed on patients in the BAT+ versus BAT− groups who belonged exclusively to the Extension BAT Cohort to establish associations between BAT presence and cardiometabolic diseases.

As the association of BAT presence with reduced prevalence of cardiometabolic disease was confirmed in the Extension BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b), we proceeded to merge the Established BAT Cohort with the Extension BAT Cohort to create an Expanded BAT Cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1a).
If a patient was present in both cohorts, data from the Established BAT Cohort were used.

blocks.html_en: To create a balanced study cohort derived from the Expanded BAT Cohort, patients in the BAT+ and BAT− groups were matched using PSM. Propensity scores were estimated using a non-parsimonious multi-variable logistic regression model with BAT status (presence or absence) as the dependent variable and age, sex, BMI and temperature at time of scan as co-variates. Matching was performed using a greedy nearest neighbour matching algorithm without replacement, with a calliper width set to 0.2 and a matching ratio of 1:2. This resulted in a final study cohort of 26,302 (8,897 BAT+ and 17,405 BAT−). Balance diagnostics were performed to assess the success of the matching procedure using standardized mean differences for all variables included in the propensity score model before and after matching. Postmatching standardized mean differences within the range of −0.10 to 0.10 indicated adequate balance between the BAT+ and BAT− groups across all measured co-variates, supporting the validity of the PSM design for causal inference.

blocks.html_en: To explore unbiased associations between BAT and other diseases, we extracted from the EHR diagnostic codes (ICD-9 and ICD-10) listed up to 1 year after the index scan from patients belonging to our PSM cohort. This left us with a final list of 511 diagnostic codes. Given the large number of codes, we initially performed a screening analysis using a univariable logistic regression analysis to identify unadjusted associations of the 511 with the presence of BAT. blocks.html_en: Machine learning approach to quantify BAT activity

sentences.en: Machine learning approach to quantify BAT activity

blocks.html_en: The 3DF workflow19 used PET and CT images in DICOM format. Using information from the DICOM header regarding image orientation and patient spatial positioning, the PET image was resampled to match the dimensions of the CT image through linear interpolation. Both PET and CT images were then converted into the .nrrd file format and processed by nnU-net. The nnU-net model produced a mask prediction where each pixel value corresponds to an anatomical site: 1 for cervical, 2 for supraclavicular, 3 for mediastinal, 4 for paraspinal, 5 for axillary and 6 for abdominal regions. The mask predictions were interpreted by 3DF, and contours were generated. These contours were down-sampled to match the original PET image dimensions, and metrics from the original PET for each anatomical site were exported to an Excel master file. The 3DF process was executed in batch mode, with several instances running simultaneously to efficiently segment a large cohort. We used this method to quantify BAT metabolic activity in 8,709 patients in the BAT+ group from our cohort. A small portion of patients (n = 188) in the BAT+ group could not be quantified due to differences in field of view between the CT and PET image.

blocks.html_en: Machine learning approach to quantify SAT and VAT area

sentences.en: Machine learning approach to quantify SAT and VAT area

blocks.html_en: The 3DF19,60 abdominal adipose tissue workflow was performed on axial CT images at the L3–L4 intervertebral disc level. The target slice was identified automatically using TotalSegmentator61 vertebral segmentation, with the analysis slice defined as the midpoint between the inferior extent of the L3 mask and the superior extent of the L4 mask. The outer body contour on the selected slice was derived by thresholding voxels above −500 Hounsfield units, followed by hole filling, removal of small components, retention of the largest connected component and morphological closing. Outer abdominal circumference was then calculated from the resulting body boundary using DICOM pixel spacing. Adipose tissue was quantified using a hybrid attenuation and AI-based method. Fat voxels were first identified within the body contour using an attenuation range of −195 to −45 Hounsfield units, and these voxels were then partitioned into SAT and VAT using TotalSegmentator tissue-type compartment masks. The outer abdominal circumference (in centimetres), SAT area (in square centimetres), VAT area (in square centimetres) and subcutaneous-to-visceral ratio were exported to an Excel master file. We used this method to quantify WAT distribution parameters in 8,040 patients with BAT from our cohort.

blocks.html_en: Multi-variable logistic regression analysis revealed that 39 out of 125 individual medications exhibited a significant association with BAT, as depicted in Supplementary Table 6. Of 38 medications examined, 29 had a positive association with the presence of BAT, suggesting that they could act as activators of this tissue. To select candidates for testing, we performed a literature search for each medication focusing on the following criteria: (1) expression of the target receptor and/or pathway in adipocytes, (2) direct effects of the medication in adipocytes and (3) potential cardiometabolic benefits beyond their intended pharmacologic effect. Out of 29 medications, losartan and valsartan fulfilled these criteria.
